newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Telecom wins some price flex - analysts.
newsitem.headline: HK Telecom wins some price flex - analysts.

text.p: Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd won official approval to offer a cut-rate international calling package for Christmas, which analysts said amounted to regulatory recognition of the company's eroding market share.

"This is a recognition by the government that the company has lost a considerable amount of market share and is no longer in as dominant a position in call origination and termination," said BZW regional telecom analyst Lloyd Fischer.
Analysts said the falling market share gave the company more freedom to set rates.
"We are approaching what the regulator describes as a 'contestable market'," he said, and Hongkong Telecom was in the process of being given more freedom to compete on prices.
Hongkong Telecom said on Wednesday the telecom regulator, the Office of the Telecommuncations Authority (OFTA), had approved the package, which will take effect December 16.
According to newspaper advertisements, registered customers for the package will get as much as 50 percent off their international telephone calls.
The company has a monopoly on International Direct Dial (IDD) calls to and from Hong Kong, and it is not allowed to lower its tariffs without prior approval from OFTA.

But Hong Kong's three new fixed-line operators are allowed to offer sharp discounts, even though they must pass IDD calls through Hongkong Telecom's network, and they are rapidly eroding the company's market share.

In November, Hongkong Telecom said it had lost 15 percent of market share in IDD calls. BZW's Fischer forecast the company could lose up to 40 percent of the IDD market by the end of fiscal year to March 31, 1997.

J.P. Morgan regional telecom analyst David Barden said the approval of the Christmas package was recognition that Hongkong Telecom is meeting the requirements set out by OFTA in levelling out the playing field.
The checklist includes interconnection agreements as well as sharing of facilities and co-location of equipment with the new fixed-line operators, which were licensed in 1995.
Barden said Hongkong Telecom has made progress in these areas and was moving towards meeting the requirements for greater tariffing freedom.
"Market dominance is part of it but it's is not the only requirement," he said.

OFTA said in a statement it has never intended to set in stone tariffing measures in developing a competitive enviroment. "Rather, it is desirable to plan for a gradual relaxation of these tariffing rules so that Hongkong Telephone Co (HKTC) could be relieved of different degrees of regulatory oversight of its tariffs as the market becomes progressively more liberal," OFTA director-general Alex Arena said.
"The ultimate objective would be to abolish all tariffs controls once a truly competitive market had been achieved," he said.
Arena said Hongkong Telecom may make submissions to OFTA should it believe it is no longer dominant and OFTA will consider such a case on its merits and according to guidelines.
He said the company has not sought to be declared non-dominant.
